Offensive Security.description: A cybersecurity discipline where trained specialists intentionally try to break into systems using the same techniques real attackers use, in order to find and fix weaknesses before criminals do.

Cyber Security.description: The broad practice of protecting computers, networks, and data from theft, damage, or unauthorized access — essentially, digital defense.

Cloud Security.description: The specific practices and tools used to keep data and systems safe when they're hosted on cloud platforms like AWS or Google Cloud, rather than on physical servers in an office.

ISO 27001.description: An internationally recognized certification showing an organization has a formal, independently audited system in place for managing and protecting sensitive information.

AWS.description: Amazon's cloud computing platform. Instead of buying and maintaining physical servers, companies rent computing power, storage, and other infrastructure from Amazon over the internet.

IaC.description: Infrastructure as Code — a practice of defining servers, networks, and other technical infrastructure using text files and code, so it can be set up automatically and consistently instead of by hand.

Kubernetes.description: An open-source system that automatically manages large numbers of containerized applications, keeping them running reliably and scaling up or down as demand changes.

Active Directory.description: Microsoft's system for managing user accounts, computers, and permissions across an organization's network — it's what decides who is allowed to log into what.

Linux Administration.description: The work of installing, configuring, and maintaining computers and servers that run Linux, a widely used operating system especially common on business and government servers.

Docker.description: A tool that packages an application together with everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same way no matter what computer it's deployed on.

Automation.description: Using scripts, tools, or software to perform repetitive technical tasks automatically, instead of someone doing them by hand every time.

Networking.description: The design, setup, and maintenance of the systems that let computers communicate with each other, whether within a single office or across the internet.

Virtualization.description: A technique that lets one physical computer act like several separate, independent ones — useful for testing, isolation, and making efficient use of hardware.

Architecture.description: The overall design and structure of a technical system — how its different parts fit together, similar to how a blueprint describes a building before it's constructed.

DB Administration.description: The ongoing work of setting up, maintaining, securing, and troubleshooting the databases that store an organization's information.

Software Development.description: Designing, writing, testing, and maintaining computer programs and applications.

Burp Suite CE.description: A widely used free tool that security professionals use to test websites and web applications for security weaknesses before attackers can exploit them.

Terraform.description: A tool that lets engineers describe the cloud infrastructure they need — servers, networks, storage — in a text file, then automatically builds it exactly as described.

Scalr.description: A platform that adds extra management, approval, and automation controls on top of Terraform for teams provisioning cloud infrastructure.

Packer.description: A tool for automatically building ready-to-use virtual machine images, so new servers can start up already configured correctly.

Windows AD.description: Microsoft's system for managing user accounts, computers, and permissions across an organization's network — it's what decides who is allowed to log into what.

OpenVPN.description: Free, open-source software that creates a secure, encrypted connection between a computer and a private network over the internet — commonly used so employees can safely access company systems remotely.

Java.description: A widely used programming language known for being able to run on almost any type of computer or device without modification.

SELinux.description: A security feature built into Linux that adds a very strict extra layer of control over what programs are allowed to do, even if one of them has been compromised.

Windows.description: Microsoft's operating system, used on the large majority of business desktop computers and many servers worldwide.

HyperV.description: Microsoft's built-in technology for running multiple virtual computers on a single physical machine.

RKE2 (Kubernetes).description: A security-hardened version of Kubernetes built by Rancher, designed for organizations with strict compliance or government security requirements.

RHEL.description: Red Hat Enterprise Linux — a paid, professionally supported version of the Linux operating system, popular in large businesses and government for its stability and support.

VMware (ESXi/vSphere).description: A widely used commercial platform for running multiple virtual computers on shared physical hardware, common in large company data centers.

Ansible.description: A tool that lets engineers automate the setup and configuration of many computers at once, using simple, readable instructions instead of doing it manually machine by machine.

Bash.description: The command-line language used to type instructions directly to a Linux or Mac computer, and to write scripts that automate repetitive tasks.

Python.description: A popular, easy-to-read programming language used for everything from simple scripts to complex data analysis and security tools.

PowerShell.description: Microsoft's command-line tool and scripting language for automating tasks and managing Windows computers.

Grafana.description: A tool that turns technical data, like server performance or network traffic, into easy-to-read charts and dashboards.

Prometheus.description: A tool that continuously collects data about how well computer systems are running, and can automatically alert engineers if something goes wrong.

OpenSearch.description: An open-source tool for storing, searching through, and analyzing large volumes of data — often used to sift through logs and security events.

Golang.description: A programming language created by Google, valued for being fast and well-suited to building reliable backend systems and infrastructure tools.

PostgreSQL (SQL).description: A free, widely trusted system for storing and organizing structured data, used behind the scenes by countless applications and websites.

Vault.description: A tool for securely storing and controlling access to sensitive information like passwords, API keys, and certificates, instead of leaving them exposed in plain text.

Linux.description: A free, open-source operating system that powers the majority of the world's servers, as well as many phones and other devices.

Ethereum.description: A public blockchain platform that lets developers build applications and financial services that run without a central company controlling them.

Algorand.description: A blockchain platform designed to process transactions quickly and cheaply, positioned as an alternative to networks like Ethereum.

Teal.description: The specific programming language used to write smart contracts — self-executing programs — on the Algorand blockchain.

Solana.description: A blockchain platform built for very high transaction speeds, commonly used for decentralized apps and finance.

TypeScript.description: A version of the JavaScript programming language with added structure and error-checking, which makes large web projects easier to build correctly.

NextJS.description: A popular framework for building fast, modern websites and web applications using the React JavaScript library.

AWS (CDK).description: A tool that lets developers define Amazon Web Services cloud infrastructure using familiar programming languages instead of a separate configuration format.

Azure.description: Microsoft's cloud computing platform, an alternative to Amazon's AWS, used by businesses to rent computing power and services over the internet.

GCP.description: Google's cloud computing platform, offering rented computing power, storage, and other services over the internet, similar to Amazon's AWS.

Jenkins.description: A widely used tool that automatically builds, tests, and deploys software whenever developers make changes, reducing manual work and human error.

Django.description: A popular framework for building websites and web applications quickly using the Python programming language.

PHP (Hack).description: A programming language created by Meta (Facebook), based on PHP, used internally to build and maintain large parts of Facebook's systems.

MySQL.description: One of the world's most widely used systems for storing and organizing structured data behind websites and applications.

Spark.description: A tool for processing very large volumes of data quickly by spreading the work across many computers at once.

React.description: A widely used JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces, originally created by Facebook/Meta.

GraphQL.description: A modern approach that lets applications request exactly the data they need from a server, avoiding wasted or unnecessary information.

Relay.description: A framework built by Meta that helps React applications efficiently fetch and manage data using GraphQL.

Python 3.description: A popular, easy-to-read programming language used for everything from simple scripts to complex data analysis and security tools.

Neo4J.description: A database designed specifically to store and query data based on relationships and connections between things, rather than in traditional rows and tables.

NestJS.description: A framework for building organized, scalable backend applications using JavaScript/TypeScript and the Node.js runtime.

MongoDB.description: A popular database that stores data in flexible, document-like structures rather than traditional rows and tables, often used in modern web applications.

Jest.description: A tool developers use to automatically test that their JavaScript code works correctly before it's released.

Skaffold.description: A Google-built tool that streamlines the process of building, testing, and deploying applications onto Kubernetes.

Google Cloud.description: Google's cloud computing platform, offering rented computing power, storage, and other services over the internet, similar to Amazon's AWS.

Node.description: A runtime that lets JavaScript, normally a language for web browsers, also run on servers — enabling JavaScript to be used for backend development.

RabbitMQ.description: Software that helps different parts of an application communicate reliably by passing messages between them, even if one part is temporarily busy or offline.

OpenShift.description: Red Hat's enterprise platform for running containerized applications on Kubernetes, aimed at large organizations needing extra support and management tools.

Cypress.description: A tool developers use to automatically test that a website works correctly by simulating real user actions like clicking and typing.

Pact.description: A tool that helps ensure different software services continue working correctly together, by testing the agreements — or 'contracts' — between them.

Salesforce.description: A widely used customer relationship management (CRM) platform that businesses use to manage sales, customers, and related data, often customized with its own development tools.

Jupyter Notebook.description: An interactive tool that lets people write and run code in small chunks alongside notes and charts, popular for data analysis and teaching.

Pandas.description: A Python library that makes it easy to organize, clean, and analyze data — similar to a very powerful spreadsheet.

matplotlib.description: A Python library used to turn data into charts and graphs.

NumPy.description: A foundational Python library for doing fast mathematical and numerical calculations, widely used in data science.

scikit-learn.description: A Python library that provides ready-made tools for building machine learning models, without needing to write the underlying math from scratch.

AngularJS.description: An older JavaScript framework (the predecessor to modern Angular) used for building interactive web applications.

Sass.description: A tool that extends standard website styling code (CSS) with extra features like variables and reusable rules, making styling large websites easier to manage.

PHP Laravel.description: A popular framework that makes it easier to build websites and web applications using the PHP programming language.

AWS services.description: Amazon's cloud computing platform. Instead of buying and maintaining physical servers, companies rent computing power, storage, and other infrastructure from Amazon over the internet.

Grunt.description: A tool that automates repetitive front-end development tasks, like combining files or optimizing images, as part of building a website.

VBA.description: A programming language built into Microsoft Office that lets people automate repetitive tasks in programs like Excel, Word, and Outlook.

VB.NET.description: A programming language from Microsoft, commonly used to build Windows desktop applications.

C#.description: A widely used, general-purpose programming language created by Microsoft, common in Windows applications, games, and enterprise software.

Advanced Excel.description: In-depth use of Microsoft Excel's more powerful features, such as formulas, macros, and automation, beyond basic spreadsheet use.

Outlook and Word Integration.description: Connecting and automating tasks between Microsoft Outlook (email and calendar) and Word (documents), often to save time on repetitive office work.
